title: Mirrors and Lenses
notes: Mirrors form images by reflection; lenses form images by refraction. Principal rays for a spherical mirror include a parallel ray reflected through F and a ray through C reflected back; for a thin lens, a parallel ray passes through (or appears from) F.

Use the proper signed equations: mirror 1/f=1/u+1/v and thin lens 1/f=1/v−1/u under the stated real-positive mirror and Cartesian lens conventions. Magnification conventions also differ: mirror m=−v/u; lens m=v/u.
Worked mirror example: concave f=15 cm and object distance u=30 cm give 1/v=1/15−1/30=1/30, so v=30 cm and m=−1: real, inverted and same size.
Worked lens example: f=+10 cm and real object u=−30 cm give 1/v=1/10−1/30=1/15, so v=+15 cm and m=−0.5: real, inverted and half-size.
Ray diagrams provide an independent check on equation signs, image orientation, size and whether the image can be caught on a screen.
confusion: Do not copy a mirror formula into a lens problem unchanged.
Simple equations assume paraxial rays and thin optical elements.

specificConditions: **Thin Lens/Mirror Approximation:** The mirror equation (1/f = 1/u + 1/v) and lens formula (1/f = 1/v - 1/u) assume thin optics where thickness is negligible. For thick lenses, principal planes must be used. Sign convention (Cartesian): distances measured from pole/lens center; positive in direction of incident light for u, opposite for v/f.

**Spherical Aberration:** Paraxial rays (close to axis) follow the simple formulas. Non-paraxial rays focus at different points, causing spherical aberration. The formulas assume paraxial approximation (small angles, sin θ ≈ θ).

**Lens/Mirror Power:** Power P = 1/f (meters) in diopters. Converging (convex lens, concave mirror): P > 0. Diverging (concave lens, convex mirror): P < 0. Powers add for thin lenses in contact: P_total = Σ P_i.
